title: A World Changed by Plague
objective: After this level you can explain how the Black Death changed wages, work and faith.
summary: With workers scarce after the Black Death, wages rose and England tried to freeze them in 1351. Fear drove flagellant processions and the false blaming and massacre of Jews, as at Strasbourg in 1349.

cards.headline: When around a third of England died, workers could name their price. Almost.
cards.body: The Black Death rewired work, pay and faith. Some of what followed was hopeful. Some was horrifying.

cards.headline: Workers become scarce, and pricey
cards.body: With so many dead, there were suddenly too few hands. The labour shortage pushed up wages for artisans and other workers, and landowners began swapping the old labour services for wages or money rents. With land cheap and pay high, many survivors lived better than before. Supply and demand, medieval edition: when workers are rare, workers cost more.

cards.headline: The lords push back
cards.body: England’s rulers tried to turn the clock back. The Statute of Labourers of 1351 tried to freeze wages at pre-plague levels and stop workers moving to find better pay. You can pass a law against arithmetic, but the arithmetic doesn’t read it.

cards.headline: Whips and repentance
cards.body: Some read the plague as God’s punishment. Groups of flagellants marched from town to town, whipping themselves to atone for their sins and calling on everyone to repent.

cards.headline: The search for someone to blame
cards.body: Fear also turned to murder. Jews were falsely accused of causing the plague by poisoning wells, and across Europe many were killed by mobs or burned. In Strasbourg, on 14 February 1349, about 2,000 Jews were burned, a city chronicler recorded. The plague only reached Strasbourg that summer. Jews were dying of the plague too, yet the accusation was widely believed. At Avignon, Pope Clement VI protected them.

cards.headline: The plague’s aftermath: understood
learned: The Statute of Labourers (1351) tried to freeze pay
Jews were falsely blamed and massacred

questions.prompt: What happened to workers’ wages after the Black Death?

options.label: They rose, because workers were scarce
They fell, because there was less work
options.rationale: Too few workers pushed pay up.

options.label: They stayed exactly the same
options.rationale: The labour shortage pushed them up.

questions.explanation: The labour shortage pushed up wages, and many survivors lived better than before.

questions.prompt: What does the Strasbourg massacre of February 1349 reveal about the accusations against Jews?

options.label: Jews there had been caught poisoning wells
Jews were killed before the plague had even reached the city
The city’s Jews had all left before the plague
The pope ordered the killings
options.rationale: Clement VI protected Jews at Avignon.

questions.explanation: About 2,000 Jews were burned in February 1349, but the plague only reached Strasbourg that summer: the accusation was false.

questions.prompt: After the plague, landowners swapped old labour services for wages or rents. Which Level 22 duty was one of those services?

options.label: Paying the tithe
options.rationale: The tithe went to the Church, not to the lord.

options.label: Carrying a knight’s armour as his squire
options.rationale: Squires were young nobles in training.

questions.explanation: Week-work, ploughing and reaping the lord’s demesne, was the kind of labour service landowners began replacing with wages or money rents.
